lesson.title: Angles: The Tilt of the World Around Us

steps.say: Imagine you're at the skate park in your neighbourhood, the way Small Number is in the story Small Number and the Skateboard Park. Every ramp there has a tilt. A gentle little ramp is easy for a beginner. A steep ramp is scary and fast. So how do we describe that tilt to a friend without waving our arms around? We measure the angle. An angle is just the amount of turn between two arms that meet at a corner, and we measure it in degrees.

visual.caption: A gentle beginner ramp: about 30 degrees

steps.say: Here's the friendly part. You already know three angles by heart, and everything else you can guess from them. Ninety degrees is the corner of a doorway, a sheet of paper, a laptop screen standing straight up. One hundred eighty degrees is a flat, straight line, like lying right down on the sidewalk. And forty five degrees is exactly half of ninety, like a ramp that goes up as fast as it goes across. These three are your reference angles.

visual.caption: Ninety degrees: the square corner, your best friend

steps.say: Now the names. If an angle is smaller than ninety degrees, we call it acute, like a sharp little pizza slice. If it is exactly ninety, it's a right angle. If it is bigger than ninety but still smaller than one hundred eighty, it's obtuse, kind of lazy and leaned back. Exactly one hundred eighty is a straight angle. And if it's bigger than one hundred eighty but less than three hundred sixty, it's reflex, the big outside turn.

visual.caption: One hundred thirty five degrees: leaned back, so obtuse

steps.say: Let's try estimating, no protractor yet. You're looking at the lid of a laptop at the library, tipped back a bit. Ask yourself, is it more or less than the straight up ninety degrees? It's tipped past straight up, so it's more than ninety. Is it flat on the table? No, not even close, so it's way less than one hundred eighty. It looks like ninety plus about a third of the rest, so I'd guess around one hundred twenty degrees. That is between ninety and one hundred eighty, so it's an obtuse angle.

visual.caption: Estimating: past 90, nowhere near 180, so about 120 degrees

steps.say: Here's a slightly harder one, and it's a skateboard trick. A skater does a spin and turns one hundred thirty degrees before landing. Their friend asks, how much of the circle did they leave behind? A full turn all the way around is three hundred sixty degrees. So the leftover big angle is three hundred sixty take away one hundred thirty, which is two hundred thirty degrees. Two hundred thirty is bigger than one hundred eighty and smaller than three hundred sixty, so that leftover is a reflex angle.

visual.caption: Two hundred thirty degrees: the big outside turn, a reflex angle

steps.say: Angles live inside shapes too. Look at a rectangle, like a hockey rink or a page in your notebook. Every single corner is a right angle, ninety degrees. Four corners, ninety degrees each, so four times ninety equals three hundred sixty degrees all together. That's why a rectangle sits so nicely flat, its corners add up to one full turn.

Triangles have a rule of their own. The three angles inside any triangle always add up to one hundred eighty degrees, a straight line. So suppose a ramp at the park makes a triangle with the ground, and two of its angles measure sixty five degrees and forty five degrees. Add those two first, sixty five plus forty five is one hundred ten. Then one hundred eighty take away one hundred ten leaves seventy degrees. Seventy is less than ninety, so that third angle is acute.

visual.caption: The missing angle: 70 degrees, and it's acute

steps.say: So next time you walk past a ramp, a road sign, or the roof of a house, try guessing its angle out loud. Compare it to forty five, ninety, and one hundred eighty, and then name it. That's really all there is to it, and you'll get quick at it fast.

visual.caption: Forty five degrees: half of a square corner

lesson.answer: Compare every angle to 45, 90, and 180 degrees: under 90 is acute, exactly 90 is right, between 90 and 180 is obtuse, exactly 180 is straight, and over 180 is reflex.

practice.question: At a skate park in Vancouver, a ramp makes a triangle with the ground. One angle is a right angle of 90 degrees, and another measures 25 degrees. How big is the third angle, and what type of angle is it?
practice.answer: 65 degrees, and it is an acute angle. (90 + 25 = 115, and 180 − 115 = 65.)
